stimuli.text: Initial-rate data for A + B → products:
A student heats 5.2 g of $$\ce{CaCO3(s)}$$, which decomposes completely: $$\ce{CaCO3(s) -> CaO(s) + CO2(g)}$$. The $$\ce{CO2}$$ is collected at 304 K and 1 atm.
The decomposition of compound X was monitored at constant temperature.
A student titrates 31.0 mL of 0.1 M weak monoprotic acid HA (Ka = 1.8 \times 10^{-5}) with 0.1 M NaOH.
2.9 g of $$\ce{NH4NO3}$$ dissolves in 60 g of water in a coffee-cup calorimeter. The temperature falls by 2.1 °C. Assume the solution's specific heat is 4.18 J/(g·°C).

A galvanic cell is made of a Mg electrode in 1.0 M $$\ce{Mg^{2+}}$$ and a Fe electrode in 1.0 M $$\ce{Fe^{2+}}$$. Standard reduction potentials: $$\ce{Mg^{2+} + 2e- -> Mg}$$ E° = -2.37 V; $$\ce{Fe^{2+} + 2e- -> Fe}$$ E° = -0.44 V.
The photoelectron spectra of Na (Z = 11) and Mg (Z = 12) are compared.

questions.stem: What is the pH of a 0.001 M solution of $$\ce{HNO3}$$ at 25 °C?

options.why: Correct. Strong acid: [H₃O⁺] equals its concentration.
Strong acids and bases ionize completely; no equilibrium is needed.

questions.stem: A reaction has a theoretical yield of 24.5 g. The actual yield is 14 g. What is the percent yield?
A reaction has a theoretical yield of 13.3 g. The actual yield is 12.8 g. What is the percent yield?
How does a catalyst increase the rate of a reaction?

options.text: It provides a pathway with a lower activation energy
options.why: Correct. The reaction goes by a different mechanism.

questions.explanation: The reaction goes by a different mechanism.

questions.stem: For $$\ce{A(g) + B(g) <=> 2C(g)}$$, K = 4.6. A mixture has [A] = 0.6 M, [B] = 0.3 M and [C] = 0.1 M. In which direction will the reaction proceed?

options.text: It proceeds forward, toward products, because Q = 0.556
It is at equilibrium, because Q = K
It proceeds in reverse, toward reactants, because Q = 0.0556
options.why: If Q is less than K, the reaction proceeds forward.

options.text: It proceeds forward, toward products, because Q = 0.0556
options.why: Correct. Q = [C]²/([A][B]) = 0.0556, which is less than K.

questions.stem: 89 g of water at 79 °C is mixed with 149 g of water at 15 °C in an insulated container. What is the final temperature?

options.why: Correct. Heat lost = heat gained; for water alone, a mass-weighted average.
Pair each mass with its own temperature.

options.why: Correct. Weight each isotope mass by its fractional abundance.

The isotopes are not equally abundant.

questions.stem: Is $$\ce{HCN}$$ polar or nonpolar, and why?

options.text: Nonpolar, because it has no polar bonds
options.why: Polarity depends on both bond polarity and geometry.
Containing H does not make a molecule polar.

options.text: Nonpolar, because its bond dipoles cancel by symmetry
options.why: Consider the molecule's shape, not only its bonds.

options.text: Polar, because its bond dipoles do not cancel

questions.explanation: HCN is linear; the dipoles do not cancel.

options.why: Divide by the reactant's coefficient too.
Correct. Multiply by the coefficient ratio 4/2.

options.why: Correct. Sum the valence electrons of all atoms, then add one per negative charge (subtract one per positive charge).

options.why: V₂ is the total final volume.

questions.stem: Which compound has the greater lattice energy, $$\ce{MgF2}$$ or $$\ce{LiF}$$?

options.text: $$\ce{LiF}$$, because its ions have larger charges
$$\ce{LiF}$$, because it has more atoms per formula unit
options.why: Number of atoms does not determine lattice energy.

options.text: $$\ce{MgF2}$$, because its ions have larger charges
options.why: Correct. By Coulomb's law, attraction increases with the product of the ion charges.

options.text: They are equal because both are ionic

questions.explanation: MgF2 has ion charges 2 and 1; LiF has 1 and 1.

questions.stem: Which bond is the most polar?

options.why: Correct. It has the largest electronegativity difference (1.8).

questions.stem: Which formula is most likely for the compound of element X (Group 2) and element Y (Group 16)?
Two buffers have the same pH, but buffer X has ten times the concentration of each component. Which is true?

options.text: Buffer X has a greater buffer capacity
options.why: Correct. More acid and base are available to react.

options.text: Buffer X has a lower pH

options.text: Buffer X cannot resist pH changes

questions.stem: Which intermolecular force is present in all molecules?

options.why: Correct. They arise from temporary dipoles in every electron cloud.
Requires H bonded to N, O or F.

questions.explanation: They arise from temporary dipoles in every electron cloud.

options.text: The one with the largest formal charges
The one with positive charge on the most electronegative atom
The one with the most double bonds
The one with formal charges closest to zero and any negative charge on the most electronegative atom

questions.stem: Samples of $$\ce{Cl2}$$, $$\ce{CO2}$$, $$\ce{O2}$$, $$\ce{CH4}$$ are all at the same temperature. Which has the highest average molecular speed?

options.why: Cl2 has a larger molar mass (70.9 g/mol).
O2 has a larger molar mass (32 g/mol).
CO2 has a larger molar mass (44 g/mol).
Correct. At the same temperature, average kinetic energy is equal, so the lightest gas moves fastest.

questions.explanation: Molar masses: Cl2 70.9, CO2 44, O2 32, CH4 16.

questions.stem: What is the rate law?

options.why: Orders are found from the data, not from coefficients.
Compare trials where only one concentration changes.
Correct. Doubling [A] multiplies the rate by 2; doubling [B] multiplies it by 4.
Recheck how the rate changes when [A] doubles.

questions.explanation: Trials 1→2: rate ×2, so order 1 in A. Trials 1→3: rate ×4, so order 2 in B.

questions.stem: A reaction has K = 46. What is K for the reaction reversed and multiplied by 2?

options.why: K is raised to a power, not multiplied.
Multiplying by n raises K to the nth power.
Correct. Reverse → 1/K; multiply by n → Kⁿ.

questions.stem: On a reaction energy profile, the reactants are at 23 kJ/mol, the transition state at 115 kJ/mol and the products at 142 kJ/mol. What is ΔH for the reaction?

options.why: Measure from the correct starting point.

questions.explanation: Forward Ea = 92, ΔH = 119, reverse Ea = -27 kJ/mol.

options.why: With L and atm, use R = 0.08206.

questions.stem: At 298 K, ΔG° for a reaction is 11 kJ/mol. What is K?

options.why: Correct. K = e^(−ΔG°/RT), with ΔG° in J/mol and R = 8.314.

questions.explanation: ln K = -4.44; K = 0.0118. Positive ΔG°: K less than 1.

questions.stem: Calculate ΔH° for $$\ce{2CO + O2 -> 2CO2}$$. (ΔH°f of O₂ is 0.)

options.why: Correct. Σ n ΔH°f(products) − Σ n ΔH°f(reactants).
Multiply each ΔH°f by its coefficient.

options.why: Use the mole fraction, not moles.

questions.stem: Why is the enthalpy of vaporization of water much larger than its enthalpy of fusion?

options.text: Vaporization separates molecules completely, overcoming all intermolecular forces

questions.stem: A weak acid HA has pKa = 11. In a solution at pH 12.3, which statement is correct?

options.why: Correct. Above the pKa, the deprotonated form dominates.

questions.stem: What is the pH of a 0.1 M solution of benzoic acid (Ka = 6.3 \times 10^{-5})?

options.why: A weak acid does not ionize completely.
Correct. Solve Ka = x²/(C − x) for x = [H₃O⁺].

questions.stem: A 15.2 mL sample of $$\ce{H2SO4}$$ is titrated to the equivalence point with 36.3 mL of 0.093 M NaOH. What is the concentration of the acid?

options.why: Correct. Each H₂SO₄ reacts with two OH⁻, so divide the moles of NaOH by 2.

questions.stem: In a Zn/Cu galvanic cell, [Zn²⁺] is increased. What happens to the cell potential?

options.why: Correct. A product's concentration rises, so Q increases.

questions.explanation: A product's concentration rises, so Q increases.

questions.stem: A reaction has K = 2 × 10⁻¹². At equilibrium:

options.text: Reactant and product concentrations are equal

questions.stem: For a reaction, ΔH° = -129 kJ/mol and ΔS° = 108 J/(mol·K). What is ΔG° at 986 K, and is the reaction favorable?

options.why: Convert ΔS from J to kJ.
Correct. ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, with ΔS in kJ/(mol·K).

questions.stem: What is the pH of a 0.1 M solution of hydrofluoric acid (Ka = 6.8 \times 10^{-4})?

options.why: A weak acid does not ionize completely.
Correct. Solve Ka = x²/(C − x) for x = [H₃O⁺].

questions.stem: When a reaction involving 0.099 mol of limiting reactant occurs in 73 g of solution (c = 4.18 J/(g·°C)), the temperature rises by 5 °C. What is ΔH for the reaction?

options.why: Divide by the moles of reactant.
Correct. q(solution) = mcΔT = 1530 J; q(reaction) = −q(solution); divide by moles.
A temperature rise means the reaction is exothermic (negative ΔH).

questions.stem: The first four ionization energies of an element are 805, 1127, 2074, 10370 kJ/mol. In which group of the periodic table is the element most likely found?

options.why: Locate the largest jump between successive ionization energies.
Locate the largest jump between successive ionization energies.
Correct. The large jump comes after removing 3 electrons, so it has 3 valence electrons.
Locate the largest jump between successive ionization energies.

questions.explanation: The big jump marks the start of removing core electrons.

questions.stem: Use the bond enthalpies to estimate ΔH for $$\ce{2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O}$$.

options.why: Correct. ΔH ≈ Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed).
Multiply each bond energy by the number of bonds.
Broken minus formed, not formed minus broken.
Bonds formed release energy: subtract them.

questions.stem: A photoelectron spectrum shows 3 peaks. From highest to lowest binding energy, their relative heights are 2 : 2 : 4. Which element is it?

options.why: Correct. The peaks correspond to $$1s^{2}\,2s^{2}\,2p^{4}$$, which has 8 electrons.

questions.stem: A weak acid (pKa 4.2) is titrated with NaOH; the equivalence point is reached at 29.9 mL. What is the pH after 15 mL of NaOH has been added?

options.why: That is only for strong acid–strong base equivalence.
Correct. At the half-equivalence point, [HA] = [A⁻], so pH = pKa.

questions.stem: A galvanic cell is built from Cu/$$\ce{Cu^{2+}}$$ and Ag/$$\ce{Ag+}$$ half-cells. Which electrode is the anode?

options.why: The higher potential is reduced at the cathode.

options.text: Ag, where reduction occurs at the anode
options.why: Reduction occurs at the cathode, not the anode.
Correct. The half-reaction with the lower reduction potential runs as oxidation at the anode.

questions.explanation: Cu (E° 0.34 V) is oxidized at the anode; Ag is reduced at the cathode.

questions.stem: A buffer contains 0.22 mol of a weak acid HA (pKa 4.74) and 0.21 mol of A⁻. What is its pH?

options.why: Correct. Cl2 is the limiting reactant.
Use the limiting reactant, which gives less product.
Apply the mole ratio from the equation.
Not all of both reactants reacts.

A compound (octane) is 84.1% C, 15.9% H by mass. What is its empirical formula?

options.why: That is the molecular formula; reduce to the simplest ratio.
Correct. Convert each percent (in 100 g) to moles and divide by the smallest.

questions.explanation: The mole ratio reduces to C4H9; the molecular formula is C8H18.

questions.stem: Reaction 1 has ΔH₁ = -388 kJ and reaction 2 has ΔH₂ = -115 kJ. A target reaction is obtained by doubling reaction 1 and reversing reaction 2. What is ΔH for the target reaction?

options.why: Enthalpies add; they do not multiply.
Reversing changes the sign of ΔH₂.
Correct. Reverse → change sign; multiply → multiply ΔH; then add.

questions.stem: The Ksp of $$\ce{AgBr}$$ is 5 \times 10^{-13}. What is its molar solubility in a solution that already contains 0.01 M of its anion?

options.why: That is the solubility in pure water.
Correct. Ksp = s(c), so s = Ksp/c.
The common ion's concentration dominates; no square root.

questions.stem: What is the pH of a 0.2 M solution of formic acid (Ka = 1.8 \times 10^{-4})?

options.why: A weak acid does not ionize completely.
Correct. Solve Ka = x²/(C − x) for x = [H₃O⁺].

parts.prompt: CaO is an ionic solid. Explain, using Coulomb's law, why CaO has a higher melting point than KCl.

rubric.criterion: Larger ion charges in CaO (2+/2−) than in KCl (1+/1−).
Greater electrostatic attraction (and smaller ions) means more energy is needed to separate the ions.

rubric.criterion: Yes; the slow step's elementary rate law matches the observed rate law.

rubric.example: The catalyst provides a new pathway.

rubric.criterion: Lower activation energy means a larger fraction of collisions are successful.

rubric.criterion: Indicator whose pKa is closest to the equivalence pH.

rubric.criterion: A⁻ reacts with added H⁺ to form HA (buffer).
rubric.example: A⁻ + H₃O⁺ → HA + H₂O, so the ratio [A⁻]/[HA] changes only slightly.

parts.prompt: Is the dissolution endothermic or exothermic? Justify.

rubric.example: Endothermic: the solution cooled, so energy was absorbed.

Calculate ΔH of dissolution in kJ/mol.

rubric.criterion: Too small, because the measured temperature change is smaller than the true change.

Calculate E°cell.

questions.title: Solubility of a slightly soluble salt

parts.prompt: Write the Ksp expression.
Calculate the molar solubility in pure water.
Calculate the molar solubility in a solution containing 0.05 M OH⁻ (from a soluble salt).
Explain how lowering the pH affects the solubility.

rubric.criterion: Correct reasoning about whether the anion is basic.
rubric.example: Solubility increases: H⁺ reacts with OH⁻ (a base), shifting the equilibrium toward dissolving.

parts.prompt: Write the electron configuration of Mg.
Explain why the 1s peak of Mg has a higher binding energy than the 1s peak of Na.

rubric.criterion: Mg has more protons, so 1s electrons are attracted more strongly (Coulomb's law).

parts.prompt: Describe one difference in the number or relative height of peaks between the two spectra.

rubric.criterion: A valid difference based on configurations.
rubric.example: Mg has one more electron, so its outermost peak is taller or an extra peak appears.

parts.prompt: Which element has the larger atomic radius? Justify using Coulomb's law.

rubric.criterion: Na: fewer protons with similar shielding, so valence electrons are held less tightly.
rubric.example: Same period; effective nuclear charge increases across.
